decisions.quote: To address this issue, we conducted the experimental study using similar design as Abrams et al. (1990) in which we introduced openly declared Bosniak (Muslim) students to five confederates who were ostensibly either of a similar ethnic origin (ingroup), different ethnic origin (out-group) or no salient ethnic origin (control group). In all conditions these confederates were strangers whom the subjects would not expect to encounter again. This experimental design allowed us to directly compare no salient identity group with standard majority influence condition from the Asch's original study (Asch, 1952) with the opportunity to test the moderating role of group similarity in conformity phenomenon.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree the study is a replication collecting new experimental data from Bosnian university students to re-test the classic Asch conformity effect and group-similarity moderation.

decisions.quote: Participants came to the laboratory for an experiment of visual discrimination. The Asch (1956) procedure was followed, adopting the standard instructions.
decisions.reason: The paper jointly cites Asch (1951, 1952, 1956) in the Introduction (line 2) as reporting the seminal 37% conformity effect, cites Asch (1952) in line 7 for the standard majority influence condition, and explicitly states in the Method (line 9) that 'The Asch (1956) procedure was followed, adopting the standard instructions' and cites (Asch, 1952, 1956) for the line judgment task (line 11). Because Asch (1956) (DOI: 10.1037/h0093718) is explicitly cited in the text for both the original conformity finding and the replicated procedure, the shipped original is supported and matches blind target 0.

decisions.quote: The results revealed a clear-cut and powerful "Asch effect". The actual proportion of conforming responses in the three experimental groups was 303 out of a possible 912 (i.e. 35.4%) and 59.2% of all subjects conformed to the erroneous judgments of confederates on at least one trial (40.8% of all subjects kept their independence). 3 Results obtained in the standard majority condition with no salient ethnic origin were quite similar to those from the original Asch study with conformity arising to 35.31%.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree the replication of the Asch conformity effect was successful; the authors explicitly report a clear-cut Asch effect (35.4% overall and 35.31% in the standard control condition) and conclude in the Discussion (line 20) that 'we replicated the Asch conformity effect.'

corrected_value.title: Knowing what to think by knowing who you are: Self-categorisation and the nature of norm formation, conformity and group polarisation
corrected_value.authors: Abrams, D., Wetherell, M., Cochrane, S., Hogg, M. A., & Turner, J. C.

decisions.quote: Consistent with the assumption of the SCT (Turner, 1991;Turner et al., 1987), participants exposed to the in-group majority showed the increase in conformity in comparison to the standard condition in which group identity was not salient. On the opposite, when the majority was presented as the out-group, the conformity effect significantly dropped. Thus, we replicated and extended past research (Abrahams et al., 1990), showing that self-categorization could play a determining role in conformity even in more minimal conditions, in which salient in-and out-group characteristics (i.e., ethnicity) were completely irrelevant for the task at hand.
decisions.reason: In addition to replicating the classic Asch conformity effect, the study explicitly adapts the design of Abrams et al. (1990) to re-test their finding that self-categorization (in-group vs. out-group majority membership) moderates conformity in the Asch paradigm without confounding similarity and competence (lines 6-7), and explicitly concludes that it replicated and extended Abrams et al. (1990) (line 22). This is an omitted target in the shipped dataset.
